Haemolytic anaemia The normal life span of an erythrocyte is about 120 days; a haemolytic state is defined as a reduction in this mean life span due to premature destruction of red cells, either intravascularly, or more commonly after sequestration by the spleen or liver. Healthy bone marrow can compensate for even quite severe haemolysis by increased erythropoi- esis; however, if the red cell survival-time is less than 15 days, or if the bone marrow is abnormal, or there is a defi- ciency of folate, iron, or other necessary nutrients, then compensation will be inadequate and haemolytic anaemia will result. In addition to typical symptoms of anaemia (above) patients frequently exhibit jaundice and splenom- egaly, while the increased erythropoiesis results in reticu- locytosis (elevated counts of immature red cells). Haemolytic anaemias may be either congenital or ac- quired. The congenital disorders include: • those due to membrane defects in the erythrocyte, such as spherocytosis or elliptocytosis • those due to enzyme defects (including the various forms of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency) • those due to haemoglobin defects (haemoglobinopa- thies), including sickle-cell disease and β-thalassaemia (below) The acquired haemolytic anaemias arise from numerous causes but may be divided into immune and non-immune types.
